I am 67 this year, and I have worked this land since I was 27. My father taught me the basics, and the rest I learned by doing it myself and watching what works. I have 16.1 mu total. Thirteen mu I do wheat in winter and maize in summer — same ground, two crops. The other 3.1 mu I grow stevia. A dealer talked me into it three years ago, and my nephew found a buyer in Shandong, so I kept it. It pays better than grain if the leaves are sweet.

For wheat, I always plant improved seed — Jimai 22 or whatever the seed station has that year. Last year I put down one full bag of compound fertilizer per mu at ploughing, that is 50 kg, and then two top dressings of urea: half a bag at green-up and another half bag at jointing. That is about 18-19 kg of nitrogen, 7-8 kg of phosphorus, and 7-8 kg of potassium per mu. I do not measure it in kilograms myself, I measure it in bags, but that is what it comes to. I irrigate three times: overwinter water if the soil is dry, once at jointing when the weather warms up, and once at grain filling. Two sprays — herbicide early, and one more for rust or aphids if they show up. I plough after maize harvest and harrow before wheat seeding. Last year I got 480 jin per mu, this year I expect the same.

For summer maize, time is short after wheat harvest. I hire a machine to plant hybrid seed, Zhengdan 958 or something like it, no-tillage straight into the wheat stubble. The machine man charges 40 yuan per mu but it saves me days of work, and at my age I cannot turn soil that fast in June heat. Fertilizer goes down with the planter: compound fertilizer base, then urea at big trumpet stage. Total about 20 kg nitrogen, 7 kg phosphorus, 6 kg potassium per mu. I irrigate twice: once in July when it gets hot and dry, and once at tasseling. Two pesticide sprays — one for weeds right after emergence, one for corn borer later. Last year 580 jin per mu. My neighbor Lao Zhang got 600, but his son helped him manage water better. I will stick with 580.

For stevia, I rotary till in spring and plant improved seedlings. Stevia needs more potassium for the sugar in the leaves, so I give it more potash than grain crops — about 12 kg nitrogen, 6 kg phosphorus, 10 kg potassium per mu. I irrigate four times because stevia roots are shallow and dry out fast. Three pesticide sprays because leafhoppers and worms love it. I harvest twice, once in summer and once in autumn. If the weather is normal, I expect 180 kg dried leaves per mu. The buyer pays by sweetness, so I cannot skip on potassium.

My neighbor Lao Zhang and I watch each other’s fields. If he changes something and his yield jumps, maybe I try it next year. But this year? Same as last year. A bad harvest means I lose real money; wasting a little fertilizer is just a cost of doing business. I would rather put down a bit too much than risk empty grain heads.
